claim: A three-level taxonomy (Code Autonomy, Pipeline Autonomy, Demand Autonomy) modeled on SAE automation levels classifies autonomous software development by which SDLC stages have moved from human responsibility to full AI control.
stance_target: framework for defining agent autonomy levels in the software factory architecture
scope_conditions: position paper proposal, not yet an industry standard
quoted_support: Inspired by the SAE automation levels, we propose and define three levels of software-development autonomy based on which stages of the software development lifecycle have moved from human responsibility to full AI control.

claim: When the same agent writes both the implementation and the tests, passing tests demonstrate consistency, not correctness — a core risk for autonomous software development quality assurance.
stance_target: pillar 1: zero-hallucination & quality control, rigid evals must be independent of the generating agent
scope_conditions: autonomous/agentic software development, any autonomy level with self-authored test suites
quoted_support: When the same agent writes the implementation and the tests, passing tests may demonstrate consistency, not correctness.

claim: The most immediate risk in current agentic software practice is 'level-skipping': teams nominally operate at Level I (human review required) while in practice merging agent-generated changes that no one has meaningfully inspected, adopting Level II practice without Level II verification or governance.
stance_target: assumption that current human-in-the-loop review practices provide real oversight
scope_conditions: organizations deploying AI coding agents in 2026
quoted_support: The most immediate risk is not an exotic fully autonomous system. It is organizations skipping levels... The team adopts Level II practices without Level II verification, governance, or accountability.

claim: A demonstration of sixteen parallel Claude agents built a working C compiler for under $20,000.
stance_target: feasibility of parallel multi-agent software construction at scale
scope_conditions: single cited demonstration, not peer-reviewed benchmark
quoted_support: In one striking demonstration, a team of sixteen parallel Claude agents built a working C compiler with under $20K.

claim: Frontier coding agents still deteriorate sharply on benchmarks testing continuous software evolution (as opposed to isolated one-shot tasks): they can add features but struggle to preserve correctness and architectural coherence across successive changes.
stance_target: claim that frontier agents are already reliably autonomous across long-horizon software maintenance
quoted_support: on benchmarks designed to test continuous software evolution rather than isolated tasks, frontier agents still deteriorate sharply: they can add features, but they struggle to preserve correctness and architectural coherence across successive changes.

claim: Higher levels of agent autonomy require assurance to shift from validating software artifacts to auditing the agent itself — its specification, skills, memory, decision provenance, communication protocols, and execution traces.
stance_target: pillar 1 + pillar 2: rigid evals must extend to agent-level audit, not just code output
quoted_support: This is why higher autonomy changes the object of assurance. Validating the software artifact is no longer sufficient. We also need to audit the agent that produced it: its specification, skills, memory, decision provenance, communication protocols, and execution traces.

claim: Autonomous agents can fork and merge execution states, share complete context, and coordinate through structured protocols at scales of thousands or millions of concurrent collaborators, which exceeds human organizational coordination limits and will require fundamentally new AI-native coordination structures rather than human-org-inspired manager/specialist/reviewer patterns.
stance_target: pillar 2/5: multi-agent coordination architecture should not simply mimic human org charts
scope_conditions: future multi-agent coordination research direction, not yet deployed at this scale
quoted_support: Autonomous agents operate under different constraints. They can fork and merge execution states, share complete context, coordinate through structured protocols, and scale to thousands or millions of concurrent collaborators.

claim: The paper's most concrete research-agenda call is for repository-scale specification-synthesis benchmarks and long-horizon evaluations of specification-implementation drift, without which claims of Level II or Level III autonomy readiness cannot be substantiated.
stance_target: state of evaluation infrastructure for autonomous software development
quoted_support: Our most concrete call: build repository-scale specification-synthesis benchmarks and long-horizon evaluations of specification-implementation drift. Without them, claims of Level II or Level III readiness cannot be substantiated.
